findings.claim: 'Using Source A, identify two reasons X gives for Y.' - the 4-mark source question in all 13 lessons.
findings.truth: The 4-mark source question in this section gives one source and asks how you know what it suggests, using the source AND contextual knowledge. 'Identify two reasons' trained a source-only answer that would score badly. All 13 converted, with rebuilt mark schemes.
findings.evidence: spec 4.4.1, Section B question table (question 1, source analysis, 4 marks, AO3)

findings.claim: 'Identify two ways in which Source F is useful...' set as '8 marks - Source Evaluation' in all 13 lessons.
findings.truth: This section sets no 8-mark source question. Its 8-mark question is the narrative account; the single-source usefulness question at 8 marks belongs to the thematic study on the other paper. All 13 converted to the 4-mark source form.
findings.evidence: spec 4.4.1, Section B question table (four questions: 4, 12, 8, 16+4 marks)

findings.claim: 'Write an essay on the question: ... Using Sources D and E and your own knowledge, evaluate the claim.' set as '16 marks - Source-Based Essay' in all 13 lessons.
findings.truth: This section's 16-mark question is a knowledge essay on a quoted statement and supplies no sources at all; it is the only question carrying the 4 SPaG marks. All 13 converted to ‘Statement.’ How far do you agree with this statement? Explain your answer - with rebuilt agree/disagree mark schemes and the SPaG line. 26 composed sources retire with them, including two modern historians (Rhodes James, Sheffield) whom this section's source questions never test.
findings.evidence: spec 4.4.1, Section B question table (question 4, essay requiring a judgement, 8 AO1 + 8 AO2 + 4 SPaG = 20)

findings.claim: 'Construct a chronological explanation of...' - the stem on all 26 narrative-account questions.
findings.truth: The 8-mark narrative question is set as 'Write an account of...'. All 26 stems converted; the tasks themselves were sound.
findings.evidence: spec 4.4.1, Section B question table (question 3, 'Write an account...')

findings.claim: 35 composed sources carried invented archive provenances - the National Archives at Kew (x6), the Imperial War Museum (x3), the Bundesarchiv and German Federal Archives (x4), the Australian War Memorial (x2), the Russian state archives, the Beatty, Sazonov, Wilson and Hankey 'Papers', the Journal des debats, the Reichstag verbatim record, and more.
findings.truth: None of these documents exists. The provenance lines are stripped so the sources read as composed extracts; a further eight invented archive citations disappear with the 16-mark rewrites.
findings.evidence: house rule on composed practice sources

findings.claim: 'examiners want...', 'the marker is looking for...', 'examiner reports flag...', 'AQA examiner reports flag...' - eight exam tips.
findings.truth: Invented exam claims. The requirement is stated without attributing it to an examiner or to an examiner report.
findings.evidence: house rule on invented exam claims

findings.claim: 'you need to identify two reasons or features clearly from the source itself... not pad your answer with own knowledge that the source does not support'
findings.truth: The tip described the wrong task AND told students not to use their own knowledge on the one source question that requires it. Rewritten for the inference-plus-context form.
findings.evidence: spec 4.4.1, Section B question 1 (AO3, source plus contextual knowledge)

findings.claim: Four comma-list answers: 'Britain, France and Russia.' (L2); 'Front-line, support and reserve trenches, linked by communication trenches.' (L7); '‘Peace, Land and Bread.’' (L12); 'Michael, Georgette, Blücher, Gneisenau and Friedensturm.' (L13).
findings.truth: All four match the validator's enumeration pattern and would reject the unit. Rewritten as single-idea cards.
findings.evidence: scripts/_validate_content_json.py, validate_flashcards (FC_ENUM_PATTERN)

findings.claim: 'An agreement carving up Persia and recognising Afghanistan and Tibet as British zones.'
findings.truth: The 1907 Anglo-Russian Convention did not make Tibet a British zone. Both powers agreed to stay out of Tibet and to respect Chinese suzerainty.
findings.evidence: Wikipedia 'Anglo-Russian Convention'

findings.claim: '...and the dreadnought race that poisoned.'
findings.truth: The description was cut off mid-sentence and shipped that way.
findings.evidence: the field itself

findings.claim: 'By 1914 Germany would build sixteen of the biggest new warships - the dreadnoughts - against Britain's twenty-nine.'
findings.truth: The two figures do not count the same thing. Britain's 29 is 20 dreadnoughts plus 9 battlecruisers; Germany's matching total is 22 (15 plus 7), not 16.
findings.evidence: Wikipedia 'Anglo-German naval arms race' (20 dreadnoughts + 9 battlecruisers vs 15 + 7)

findings.claim: Paul Kennedy, 'The Rise of Anglo-German Antagonism' (content_html and a flashcard).
findings.truth: The book is 'The Rise of the Anglo-German Antagonism, 1860-1914' (1980).
findings.evidence: standard citation of Kennedy 1980

findings.claim: Source B dates Bülow's 'place in the sun' speech to 'the Reichstag in December 1899'; the chronology model answer repeats it and lists it after 1898.
findings.truth: Bülow made the speech on 6 December 1897, as German Foreign Secretary - as the lesson's own article text says. Both corrected, and the model answer resequenced.
findings.evidence: Wikipedia 'Weltpolitik' (6 December 1897, German Foreign Secretary)

findings.claim: '...three pre-war shocks that hardened the.'
findings.truth: The description was cut off mid-sentence and shipped that way.
findings.evidence: the field itself

findings.claim: Q: 'Which two states alone supported Germany at Algeciras?' A: 'Germany was supported only by Austria-Hungary.'
findings.truth: The question asks for two and the answer names one. Question and answer aligned on the single supporter.
findings.evidence: the card itself; the article text says 'only Austria-Hungary's support'

findings.claim: Four exam tips (L5, L8, L12, L13) coach a '16-mark Source-Based Essay' and tell students to 'use both sources as launch points'. None mentions the SPaG marks.
findings.truth: The 16-mark question supplies no sources; all its evidence must come from the student's own knowledge, and it is the only question in the section that carries 4 further marks for spelling, punctuation and grammar. All four rewritten.
findings.evidence: spec 4.4.1, Section B question 4 (essay, SPaG marks available)

findings.claim: 'The German government's spokesman admitted: ‘the war is now lost’'
findings.truth: The remark that the war was lost is attributed to Moltke speaking to the Kaiser, and even that wording is disputed. No government spokesman said it.
findings.evidence: Wikipedia 'First Battle of the Marne' (the alleged 'Your Majesty, we have lost the war'; the article notes it is uncertain)

findings.claim: '3 August 1914: Germany declared war on France and demanded passage through Belgium.'
findings.truth: The ultimatum to Belgium was delivered on 2 August 1914, the day before the declaration of war on France. Split into two bullets.
findings.evidence: Wikipedia 'German invasion of Belgium (1914)'

findings.claim: 'a 1925 memoir by German general Alexander von Kluck'
findings.truth: Kluck's account of the 1914 campaign was published in 1920 (English translation 1923). The mark scheme's 'more than a decade later' followed from the wrong date.
findings.evidence: standard bibliography of Kluck, 'Der Marsch auf Paris und die Marneschlacht' (1920)

findings.claim: 'An extract from a 1928 memoir by Field Marshal Sir Douglas Haig, recalling the Battle of the Somme'
findings.truth: Haig published no memoir. He died in January 1928 and his diaries and papers appeared only after his death. A composed extract was presented as a book he wrote. Recast as a diary entry of November 1916, and the mark scheme's provenance comment with it.
findings.evidence: Haig died 29 January 1928; his private papers were published from 1952 (Blake)

findings.claim: 'fired around one million shells in eight hours along an eight-mile front' (article and model answer)
findings.truth: The opening bombardment at Verdun on 21 February 1916 ran for about ten hours.
findings.evidence: Wikipedia 'Battle of Verdun' ('A 10-hour artillery bombardment by 808 guns')

findings.claim: 'French counter-attacks in October and December retook Forts Douaumont and Vaux.'
findings.truth: Fort Douaumont was retaken on 24 October 1916 and Fort Vaux on 2 November 1916, not in December.
findings.evidence: Wikipedia 'Fort Vaux' ('2 November 1916, the fort is recaptured')

findings.claim: Falkenhayn's December 1915 memorandum described as 'drawn from German military archives published after the war'.
findings.truth: No copy of the so-called Christmas Memorandum survives. It is known only from Falkenhayn's own post-war account. Presenting it as an archived document overstates the evidence.
findings.evidence: Wikipedia 'Battle of Verdun' ('According to his memoirs written after the war...'; the document is known only from postwar sources)

findings.claim: 'over four million shells fired in two weeks, ten times the weight delivered before the Somme'
findings.truth: The Somme preliminary bombardment fired about 1.5 million shells and Third Ypres about 4.25 million - under three times as many. 'Ten times' is not supportable.
findings.evidence: the lesson's own Somme figure (L7/L8: 1.5 million shells) against 4.25 million at Third Ypres

findings.claim: 'Churchill resigned from the Admiralty in May 1915 and went to fight on the Western Front.'
findings.truth: Churchill did not resign from the Admiralty. He was moved out of it in the coalition reshuffle of May 1915, stayed in the government until November 1915, and reached the Western Front in 1916.
findings.evidence: Wikipedia 'Winston Churchill' (replaced as First Lord by Balfour, 25 May 1915)

findings.claim: 'The 1909 Declaration of London required warships stopping a merchant vessel to give the crew time to abandon ship...'
findings.truth: The Declaration of London was never ratified by any state and never came into force, so it required nothing. The cruiser rules came from customary prize law.
findings.evidence: Wikipedia 'Declaration of London' ('no state ever ratified the declaration and consequently it never came into force')

findings.claim: 'killing 1,198 passengers, including 128 American citizens' (article and a flashcard)
findings.truth: 1,198 is the total of passengers and crew, not passengers alone.
findings.evidence: standard Lusitania casualty figure

findings.claim: 'the Kiel naval mutiny of October 1918' (L11), 'On 28 October... sailors at Kiel mutinied' (L13), and the date repeated in the L13 conclusion, two mark schemes and a flashcard.
findings.truth: The Kiel mutiny ran from 3 to 11 November 1918. Scheer's sortie order was issued on 24 October and the first refusals came at Wilhelmshaven on 29-31 October. Corrected in all seven places.
findings.evidence: Wikipedia 'Kiel mutiny' (3-11 November 1918; Wilhelmshaven refusals 30-31 October; order of 24 October)

findings.claim: Source B: a memorandum of 27 June 1917 in which 'Admiral Sir John Jellicoe' urges the War Cabinet to adopt convoys against 'the Admiralty's reluctance'.
findings.truth: Jellicoe was the leading opponent of convoying, not its advocate - as the lesson's own article says ('The Royal Navy was initially against convoying... Junior officers and David Lloyd George disagreed'). The first convoy had also already sailed by 27 June. Reattributed to an Admiralty anti-submarine staff officer writing in April 1917, and the mark scheme with it.
findings.evidence: the lesson's own content_html; standard account of the convoy decision of April-May 1917

findings.claim: 'Examiner reports flag this misconception every year.' - inside the article text.
findings.truth: Invented exam claim, and inside content_html rather than an exam tip. Removed.
findings.evidence: house rule on invented exam claims

findings.claim: 'By April... Haig issued the famous ‘backs to the wall’ order. In response, on 26 March 1918 the Allies appointed French general Marshal Ferdinand Foch as Generalissimo...'
findings.truth: The sequence is reversed: Foch was appointed on 26 March, sixteen days before Haig's order of 11 April, which cannot have caused it. Foch was also not made a Marshal of France until August 1918. Both corrected; the lesson's own model answer already had 11 April right.
findings.evidence: Doullens Conference 26 March 1918; Haig's Special Order of the Day, 11 April 1918

findings.claim: 'Ludendorff resigned on 27 October 1918.'
findings.truth: Ludendorff left office on 26 October 1918.
findings.evidence: Wikipedia 'Erich Ludendorff' (in office to 26 October 1918)

findings.claim: Source F: 'a private letter by Italian foreign minister Tommaso Tittoni... dated November 1902'.
findings.truth: The Italian foreign minister in November 1902 was Giulio Prinetti, who held the post from 1901 to 1903 and made the secret neutrality agreement with France that the source describes. Tittoni took over in November 1903.
findings.evidence: Wikipedia 'Giulio Prinetti' (foreign minister 1901-1903)

findings.claim: Source F attributes 'I beg you in the name of our old friendship to do what you can to stop your allies from going too far' to '[Wilhelm to Nicholas]'.
findings.truth: That line is Nicholas to Wilhelm, sent at 1 a.m. on 29 July 1914. The attribution was reversed on a real, quotable telegram. Corrected, with Wilhelm's genuine reply ('exerting my utmost influence') in its place.
findings.evidence: Wikipedia 'Willy-Nicky correspondence' (sender Nicholas II, 29 July 1914)

findings.claim: Source F: 'German staff officer Captain Friedrich von Lossberg... touring the Somme front line in late September 1916'.
findings.truth: Lossberg was a lieutenant-colonel in 1916 and chief of staff of the German Second Army on the Somme, not a captain.
findings.evidence: Wikipedia 'Fritz von Lossberg' (promoted lieutenant-colonel January 1915; chief of staff, 2nd Army, from the opening of the Somme)

findings.claim: Source F, dated August 1911: 'The Cabinet has authorised cooperation with the French navy in the Mediterranean.'
findings.truth: No such Cabinet authorisation existed in August 1911. The Mediterranean/Channel division of labour was settled in 1912, as the question's own model answer says. Softened to Admiralty planning.
findings.evidence: the question's own mark scheme ('The 1912 Anglo-French Naval Convention formalised exactly this arrangement')

findings.claim: Source F: '8 per cent by gas' among British trench casualties in November 1916.
findings.truth: Gas accounted for a very small share of British battle casualties - a fraction of one per cent of wounds across the war, not 8 per cent. Reduced to 2 per cent and the residual rebalanced so the figures sum to 100.
findings.evidence: British Army wound-cause statistics (shell and mortar ~59%, small arms ~39%, gas well under 1%)

findings.claim: Source A: 'the diary of Australian Sergeant Walter Downing of the 5th Brigade AIF'.
findings.truth: Walter Downing is a real, published Australian soldier-author ('To the Last Ridge'), and he served in the 57th Battalion, 15th Brigade - not the 5th. A composed diary entry should not be hung on a named real writer with the wrong unit. De-named.
findings.evidence: standard biography of W. H. Downing, 57th Battalion AIF

findings.claim: All 13 twelve-mark stems read 'Evaluate the usefulness of Sources B and C to a historian studying X. Use the sources and your knowledge of the period in your answer.'
findings.truth: The task, sources and marks are all correct, so I left the wording alone. The board's own stem is 'How useful are Sources B and C to an historian studying X? Explain your answer using Sources B and C and your contextual knowledge.' Options: (a) leave as is - the demand is identical; (b) reword all 13 to the board's phrasing so students meet the exact wording they will see. I recommend (b) as a cheap follow-up, but it is a style call, not a correction.
findings.evidence: spec 4.4.1, Section B question 2 ('How useful are sources...')
findings.ruling: Task is right; reword the 12-mark stems to the board wording in the fleet-wide stem sweep (relabel queue).

findings.claim: Every source in this unit is composed - 52 after the 16-mark rewrites - written in the voice of real people (Delcasse, Crowe, Grey, Izvolsky, Joffre, Kluck, Haig, Jellicoe, Scheer, Ludendorff, Hankey, Buchanan, Page).
findings.truth: Stripping the invented archive citations removes the false claim that these documents are held somewhere, but the extracts still put invented words in real mouths. Options: (a) accept them as clearly composed teaching sources, which is what most published revision material does; (b) replace them over time with genuine extracts, which exist for many of these figures (Joffre's order of the day, Haig's Somme despatch, the Holtzendorff memorandum, the Willy-Nicky telegrams, Lloyd George at the Mansion House - several are already near-verbatim here). I recommend (a) now and (b) as a slow background job, prioritising the 4-mark sources students quote from.
findings.evidence: house rule on composed practice sources
findings.ruling: Composed sources accepted (provenances stripped); replace 4-mark ones with genuine extracts in the source-bank pass.

findings.claim: 'Six young assassins from the secret Serbian society the Black Hand had crossed the border to kill him.'
findings.truth: The Sarajevo group belonged to Young Bosnia and were armed and trained by Black Hand members; only three of them (Princip, Grabez, Cabrinovic) crossed from Serbia, the rest being local Bosnians. The lesson's own glossary already says the Black Hand 'trained and armed' them, and 'the Black Hand' is the standard GCSE shorthand, so I have not changed it.
findings.evidence: Wikipedia 'Assassination of Archduke Franz Ferdinand'

findings.claim: 'the French contribution shrank from 40 divisions to 16'
findings.truth: The French Sixth Army fielded 13 divisions against 20 British on 1 July 1916; other counts give 11 or 16 depending on what is included. The '40 to 16' figure is within the range textbooks use, so I have not changed it.
findings.evidence: Wikipedia 'Battle of the Somme' ('13 divisions in the Sixth Army, against 20 British divisions')

findings.claim: Source C: 'Some 13,000 prisoners and 200 guns were taken' at Amiens on 8 August 1918.
findings.truth: Prisoner counts for the first day range from 13,000 (Fourth Army) to over 15,000 (all Allies); gun captures are usually given nearer 400 than 200. No single authoritative day-one gun figure was found, so I have left it.
findings.evidence: Wikipedia 'Battle of Amiens (1918)' (over 15,000 prisoners day one; 500 guns by 27 August)

findings.claim: 'The treaty bound each state to come to the others' aid if attacked by two or more Great Powers.'
findings.truth: That is Article III of the Triple Alliance only. Article II also bound Germany and Austria-Hungary to help Italy if France attacked her unprovoked, and Italy to help Germany in the same case. The lesson's summary is incomplete rather than wrong, and it is the usual GCSE simplification.
findings.evidence: text of the Triple Alliance of 1882

summary: All 13 lessons carry findings. The exam layer was the main problem: 65 of the 78 practice questions were set in forms this section does not use - 13 source-based 16-mark essays (it supplies no sources and carries the 4 SPaG marks), 13 eight-mark source-evaluation questions (no such question exists), 13 four-mark 'identify two reasons' questions (the real question asks how you know, using contextual knowledge) and 26 'construct a chronological explanation' stems. Nine exam tips carried invented examiner claims, one of them inside content_html and one telling students not to use their own knowledge on the question that requires it. 35 composed sources carried invented archive provenances. The factual layer is mostly sound but not clean: seven HIGH corrections, including the Kiel mutiny dated 28 October rather than 3 November in seven places, Jellicoe cast as the advocate of convoying he actually opposed, a Willy-Nicky telegram attributed to the wrong emperor, a 1928 Haig memoir that does not exist, Bulow's 'place in the sun' speech dated 1899, and Foch's appointment made a response to an order given sixteen days later. Two truncated descriptions and four comma-list flashcards would have failed the validator. 194 edits.
